---
title: "Performance"
---

phplyr is a thin layer. Each verb calls one or two methods of the table it is
given, so the backend determines how fast a pipeline runs. This page reports
timings for phibble's shared benchmark workloads on DataFrame and SQLite, and for
three phplyr pipelines on DataFrame, PolarsTable, and SQLite, and gives guidance
on choosing a backend.

## Method

`bench/harness.php` runs each workload twice: as a phplyr pipeline, and as the
same calls made directly on the table. `bench/generate.php` writes the data. It
is the same generator and seed as phibble's `bin/bench`, so the two harnesses
time identical data:

- `events.csv`: 1,000,000 rows of `id`, `key` (10,000 distinct values), `g`
  (8 labels), `x` (float, about 2% NA), and `t` (datetime).
- `dims.csv`: 100,000 rows of `key`, `label`, and `w`.

```bash
php bench/generate.php 1000000
php bench/harness.php --backend=frame --runs=3
php bench/harness.php --backend=sqlite --runs=3
```

Each timing includes `collect()`, so lazy backends do their work inside the
timer. The numbers below are medians of three runs on an Apple Silicon Mac with
PHP 8.5 and phibble fa978f6.

## phplyr's overhead

At 100,000 rows, the phplyr pipeline and the direct calls differed by at most
5% on every workload and backend, which is within run-to-run noise. Grouped
slices, `pivot_*()`, and `complete()` build on the same table methods and carry
the same small overhead.

## Timings at 1,000,000 rows

| Workload | DataFrame (s) | SQLite (s) |
| --- | --: | --: |
| Grouped `summarise()` of `n()`, `mean()`, and `sum()` by `key` | 0.13 | 0.39 |
| The same with closures | 0.58 | 2.11 |
| Grouped `arrange(t)`, then `mutate()` with `lag()`, `cumsum()`, and `row_number()` | 0.99 | 4.78 |
| `filter(col('x')->gt(0)->and(...))` | 0.47 | 0.34 |
| The same filter as a closure | 0.51 | 2.32 |
| `mutate()` with two expressions | 0.26 | 2.29 |
| `left_join()` of 1M × 100k rows on `key` | 0.33 | 2.44 |
| `arrange(desc('x'), 'id')` | 0.67 | 2.33 |
DataFrame peaked at about 1.5 GB of memory for the 1M-row table and its results.

## Choosing a backend

- **In-memory `DataFrame`** suits data that fits in memory, up to a few million
  rows. Expression arguments are the fastest form: a grouped summary with
  `mean('x')` runs about four times faster than the same summary written as
  closures, because phibble computes it in one pass without building a table
  per group.
- **A database table (`Phibble\tbl()`)** avoids loading the data into PHP.
  With expressions, `filter()` and `summarise()` run in the database, and only
  the result reaches PHP, so memory stays small. This is the right choice when
  the data lives in a database or doesn't fit in memory. For data already in
  memory, a frame is faster: these timings exclude loading, and reading the 1M-row
  CSV into a frame takes about 1.4 seconds. Pipelines that return every row
  (`mutate()`, `arrange()`, unfiltered joins) spend most of their database time
  transferring rows to PHP.
- **Closures on a database table** load all rows first and then run in memory.
  Use `col()` expressions and phplyr's helpers to keep the work in SQL.
- **SQLite columns need declared types.** PDO binds values as strings. In an
  untyped column, SQLite stores them as text and compares numbers as text.

- **PolarsTable** (phibble's Polars backend, on the phpolars extension) runs the verbs in Polars, 10 to 100 times faster
  than DataFrame, and pays mainly for bringing rows back into PHP. See below.

## PolarsTable

`bench/backends.php` times three phplyr pipelines on DataFrame, PolarsTable, and
SQLite, and checks that all three backends return the same rows. It is adapted
from phpolars' benchmark script. The pipelines are:

- **A:** filter, join a store lookup, two-key summarise, then a ranking window.
- **B:** grouped `lag(order_by:)`, `cumsum()`, and a share of the group total
  over all rows.
- **C:** pipeline A with a closure in `filter()`.

Times are the best of three runs through `collect()`, on an Apple M5 Ultra with
Homebrew PHP 8.5, phibble 0.3.0, and Polars 0.55.2 at two threads. In every case the
three backends returned the same rows. The full results, with all repeat
timings and version details, are in
[`benchmarks/backends-results.json`](benchmarks/backends-results.json).

`bench/backends.R` runs pipelines A and B with dplyr 1.2 on the same data,
and checks that dplyr's row counts and column sums match phplyr's. Its
results are in [`benchmarks/dplyr-results.json`](benchmarks/dplyr-results.json).
Pipeline C has no dplyr version, because its closure is PHP code.

| Pipeline, 1M rows | DataFrame (s) | PolarsTable (s) | SQLite (s) | dplyr (s) |
| --- | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| A: reduce to a ranked summary | 0.75 | 0.05 | 0.43 | 0.07 |
| B: windows over every row | 1.25 | 0.42 | 3.33 | 0.02 |
| C: A with a closure | 1.13 | 0.87 | 2.01 | |

dplyr runs these pipelines in compiled code. On A, which reduces the data
before collecting, PolarsTable (0.05 s) and dplyr (0.07 s) take about the
same time. On B, which returns every row, dplyr is the fastest by a wide
margin.

The verbs themselves are fast in Polars. Most of PolarsTable's time goes to
converting results back to PHP values: about 0.2 seconds per million rows of
plain columns, plus about 0.5 seconds per million values of a datetime column,
because each value becomes a PHP `DateTimeImmutable`. A pipeline that returns
every row of a table with a datetime column can therefore be slower on
PolarsTable than on DataFrame. In phibble's harness, `mutate()` and `left_join()`
returning 1M rows took 1.3 seconds on PolarsTable against 0.3 seconds on
DataFrame.

A closure makes PolarsTable convert the data to a DataFrame and back, which costs
about a second per million rows. Pipeline C runs its closure step that way.

Use PolarsTable when a pipeline reduces the data before collecting
(summaries, filters, `distinct()`, or a join followed by a summary), when it
chains several steps, or when the data starts in Polars:
`PolarsTable::fromPolars(Phpolars\read_csv($path))` skips phibble's CSV parse.
Keep the pipeline in expressions so every step stays in Polars.
